title: The Oldest Manuscript of The Song of Roland Is Actually an English Performance Copy
dek: The Oxford Digby 23 manuscript is written in Anglo-Norman, and scholars date it to between 1140 and 1170 by the degree of dialect drift — the most complete version of this French epic was performed for the English.
why: This is a members-only sample episode, medium information density, but it gets very concrete about how a manuscript gets read as "some minstrel's working copy" — good for listeners interested in manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction.
who: Listeners interested in medieval manuscripts, oral epic and dialect reconstruction; anyone who wants to see how a single manuscript gets reconstructed into a specific performance setting.
skip: If you only want the political subtext of The Song of Roland, you can skip it — that part is in the next episode.

points.h: The most complete version is an English manuscript
points.body: The Song of Roland is a French epic that took shape around the 12th century, belonging to the genre Chanson de Geste (songs of deeds), and it spread with 12th-century French cultural hegemony to regions including Britain. But its most complete and oldest surviving version is not from France proper — it is an English manuscript, catalogued as Oxford Digby 23. This manuscript was at some point bound together with a completely unrelated book, which is why it is called Digby 23 B, and A is that "other book." Nobody knows who bound them together; possibly some monk felt both were his favourite books.

points.h: Every stanza is a camera position
points.body: The poem is organised in laisses (stanzas) of varying length, and each laisse is like a camera focus: when the scene or the mood changes, you change laisse. The whole poem is in decasyllabic meter, cut at performance into four plus six: the first four syllables rise, then a dramatic pause, then the last six fall, overall close to iambic turning into trochaic. Chanted over and over it becomes hypnotic, and the poem runs to four thousand lines — hours of recitation.

points.h: At peak emotion, the same action is performed three times
points.body: This kind of epic has a convention that is hard for any reteller to handle: when the action is especially violent or the emotion especially strong, several consecutive laisses will tell the same action from three angles — a slow-motion sequence in poetic form. Roland's refusal to blow the oliphant, for instance, is told three times with almost no gap between them. This is also why it reads like an action film or a comic: scenes cut hard, with no softening transition — "Roland dies, his soul ascends" is followed directly by "the Emperor arrives at Roncesvalles."

points.h: The end of the manuscript preserves the performer's name
points.body: Digby 23 is very likely a real minstrel's working copy. Line 4002 of the poem, its final line, says roughly: "here ends the song of deeds; Turoldus will tell no more." This line comes before Charlemagne's lament, so it reads more like the performer saying: this is too sad, I cannot go on. The name Turoldus does not appear in the poem and is not a known scribe, so scholars lean towards him being the owner of this manuscript, the performer of this repertoire.

points.h: Pocket-book dimensions give away that it was for work
points.body: The manuscript measures only about six and a half inches by four and a half — a pocket book you could carry on your person, not a rich man's finely bound volume. It is itself heavily worn and not refined, and it contains some small annotations of unclear meaning. Together these features point to an itinerant professional performer: he might have travelled alone with an instrument, or been the lead singer or narrator in a troupe, with someone in front of him doing the physical acting. Such people were jongleurs — the origin of the later word juggler.

points.h: The dialect pins this performer to England
points.body: The manuscript is not in the French of central France, nor of the continent, but in Anglo-Norman, which suggests the performer was probably Anglo-Norman, performing in Britain or at least in Normandy. The dialect features are very specific: continental French O and OU are replaced by U, so Roland becomes Rulant and l'or becomes l'ur; Anglo-Norman French is also losing final soft e. These changes even begin to break the originally strict decasyllabic meter, leaving some lines with only nine syllables or swelling to eleven.

points.h: Accent drift alone can date a manuscript
points.body: Scholars' grasp of this dialect is fine enough that they can date the manuscript to between 1140 and 1170 based on the degree of accent drift. The method is similar to scholars reconstructing Shakespearean pronunciation, tracking regular changes in syllables and sounds. Poetry is especially suited to this reconstruction, because meter and rhyme expose which sounds were dropped and which were added. For many jongleurs, French was a second language anyway, spoken with a dialect accent — and they spelled by sound.

points.h: A French epic, an English artefact
points.body: Although this is a French poem about an old French king, the manuscript is an English thing, performed for Britons in its day. There is no equally complete other manuscript to compare line by line, but there are abundant records of The Song of Roland being sung before and after this copy, and scholars can use them to judge where this performer departs from what the genre should look like. The episode goes on to cover the poem's symbolic system, how its audience is constructed, and what the music sounds like.
